biggest_catch: This route does not promise money at all — it promises a directory. Everything depends on your state's programs, their current funding, and their deadlines. A program listed on DSIRE may be exhausted, paused, or ended (the 2025-2026 federal funding disruptions froze several state-run rebate programs), so a listing is a lead, not an offer. You must verify each program on the state energy office's or utility's own page — with its last-update date — before spending a dollar or counting on a rebate. Nothing here is income; at best it is a discount on purchases you were already going to make.
catches: DSIRE entries can go stale: the solarenergyworld.com 2026 guide warns 'Always verify the last update date... If a page appears outdated, follow the website link provided for the most recent details.'
Programs are funding-limited and first-come; several state programs were paused in 2025 during federal funding freezes and may not have resumed.

NASEO's site represents the 56 state/territory energy offices and their directors — it is an association resource, not a rebate application portal; you still apply through the individual state office.
The catalog's own examples need care: federal IRA-era rebate programs (HOMES/HEEHRA) are state-administered and were never universal; treat legacy mentions skeptically.

DOE's FY2026 enacted budget keeps the Weatherization Assistance Program ($9.6M) and State Energy Program ($4.5M) funded — these flow through state energy offices but are grants to states, not direct consumer checks.
The route overlaps R0315/R0321 in method (look up your utility); its unique value is catching state-level programs utilities don't list.

c1.evidence: NASEO (National Association of State Energy Officials) is a real nonprofit founded 1986, Arlington VA, representing the 56 state/territory energy directors — active in 2026 (affiliate-program doc updated January 5, 2026, naseo.org). DSIRE is operated by the N.C. Clean Energy Technology Center at NC State, funded by DOE, live since 1995.

c2.evidence: N.C. Clean Energy Technology Center's DSIRE page: 'summaries of more than 2,600 incentives and policies, used by over 180,000 different people each month.' DSIRE April 2026 solar-incentives summary: 'Incentives for Solar Photovoltaics are available in 45 states + DC.' Modernize guide (updated Aug 12, 2026): DSIRE 'allows you to search through policies and incentives by state and zip code.'

c3.evidence: Searching DSIRE and the NASEO directory is free — no fee, account, or purchase required. Individual programs may require purchases, but the route itself costs nothing.

c4.evidence: The catalog claims no fixed payout ('Varies by program'), and the evidence confirms a live, current directory of 2,600+ incentives — the honest claim the route actually makes is verified.

eligibility: Varies by program. Generally: resident of the state/territory, and each listed program sets its own rules (homeowner vs renter, income caps for low-income programs, utility customer status).

steps: Open the DSIRE database via the N.C. Clean Energy Technology Center page at https://nccleantech.ncsu.edu/renewable-energy-resources/dsire/ (or find your state energy office through the NASEO member network at https://naseo.org).
Select your state (or enter your ZIP code) and filter for the incentive type you want — rebates, tax credits, loan programs, weatherization.
Read each listing's summary AND its last-update date; skip anything that looks stale or whose funding status is unclear.

Click through to the official program page (state energy office or utility) and verify the current terms, eligibility, funding status, and application deadline — do not apply based on the DSIRE summary alone.
Apply through the program's own official application before its deadline, keeping receipts and documentation as that program requires.
timing: Varies by program — each state/utility program sets its own application windows and processing times; always confirm the deadline on the program's official page.
